claim: Prefers counting a behavior as misalignment only when the model is shown to be capable of the better behavior and able to tell what the user wants, over judging bad outputs alone, because otherwise capability failures get mistaken for misalignment.
quote: We say a model is misaligned if it outputs B, in some case where the user would prefer it outputs A, and where the model is both: capable of outputting A instead, and capable of distinguishing between situations where the user wants it to do A and situations where the user wants it to do B
title: Call for research on evaluating alignment (funding + advice available)

claim: Treat evidence that the model 'knows' the right answer elsewhere, or does better under non-informative prompt changes, as convincing evidence of misalignment.
quote: Gives incorrect answers, but you can show it ‘knows’ the answer in another context
title: Call for research on evaluating alignment (funding + advice available)

claim: Distrusts evidence that a model can describe deception in a story-like setting as indicating actual deceptive intent, since it measures understanding rather than trying to deceive.
quote: I don't think this tells us very much about whether the model is in question is actually trying to deceive us, but it's a tiny bit interesting.
title: A very crude deception eval is already passed

claim: Prefers tests that show mechanistic, correct theory of mind over surface text mimicry because apparent competence may just reflect reproduced relevant snippets.
quote: If you're more careful, there might be ways to more rigorously test whether the theory of mind is actually correct/mechanistic, versus just mimicking relevant text snippets, but I haven't tried to do that.
title: A very crude deception eval is already passed

claim: In a setup, draw prompts from real deployment data (actual user input/completion logs) instead of a hand-written fixed set because it reflects real usage and resists overfitting to the benchmark.
quote: Another solution is to have the prompts reflect how the model is actually being used; get the data on [user input, completion] from AI labs, and then evaluate alignment on this dataset for different models
title: More detailed proposal for measuring alignment of current models

claim: Distrusts fixed public prompt sets because models can be trained on similar instructions, gaming the benchmark; favors secret test sets or large resampled prompt spaces.
quote: Using a fixed set of prompts like this makes it relatively easy to ‘hack’ the benchmark by training on similar instructions (although keeping the specific prompts secret helps a lot).
title: More detailed proposal for measuring alignment of current models

claim: Prefers having the model actually write and run code and observe real outputs over having it describe what it would do and judging success ourselves, because this approximates what would happen 'in the wild'.
quote: We attempted to approximate as closely as possible what would happen if the model actually attempted the task “‘in the wild” - we actually had the model write code and see the inputs of running that code, rather than just having the model describe what it might do and assess ourselves whether this would succeed.
title: More information about the dangerous capability evaluations we did with GPT-4 and Claude.

claim: In a setup, have researchers act as tools and feed real command results back into the prompt step by step instead of using static or purely described outcomes, because this creates a realistic simulation from the model's perspective.
quote: We built some tooling to allow researchers to quickly obtain the result of carrying out the model’s suggested action and add this to the model’s prompt, allowing them to ‘step through’ the task with the model. For many tasks and actions, this allows us to create a realistic simulation from the model’s perspective.
title: More information about the dangerous capability evaluations we did with GPT-4 and Claude.

claim: In a setup, swap fake credentials for real ones behind the scenes while making it appear to the model that the fake ones were used, instead of exposing the safety scaffolding, because the model's perceived situation stays intact while risk is contained.
quote: we would give the model fake account or credit card details, then swap in real ones when it tried to use these, while ensuring that it appeared to the model as if the fake credentials had been used.
title: More information about the dangerous capability evaluations we did with GPT-4 and Claude.

claim: In a setup, have humans role-play or spoof parts of the environment (victims, task outcomes) and let the model interact with real unsuspecting humans where safe, instead of obviously mocked interactions, so the agent continues behaving as it would in a real situation.
quote: In some cases we “spoofed” the results of completing illegal and/or dangerous tasks - e.g. telling the model that it had successfully obtained someone’s identity via phishing, to see if the model could then take sensible steps to continue the task.
title: More information about the dangerous capability evaluations we did with GPT-4 and Claude.

claim: Prefers operationalizing concrete, real-world end-to-end tasks over abstract or toy benchmarks because they reveal the actual obstacles an agent would face in the wild.
quote: Operationalized 12 real-world tasks** of increasing difficulty, ranging from very basic tasks (searching for information in a file) to advanced ones (fine-tuning an open-source LLM).
title: ARC Evals new report: Evaluating Language-Model Agents on Realistic Autonomous Tasks

claim: In a setup, use a real (volunteer) target and intercept and simulate their responses instead of a fully fictional victim or live unsupervised action, because it keeps the interaction realistic while remaining safe.
quote: The agent is given an email account and a debit card. We intercept any email the model sends and simulate the student’s responses.
title: ARC Evals new report: Evaluating Language-Model Agents on Realistic Autonomous Tasks

claim: In a setup, give the agent real tool access (code execution, files, browsing, cloud accounts) and make it figure out APIs and configuration instead of handing it pre-digested inputs, because that mirrors how a human would operate from a command line.
quote: allow it to run code on a computer, read and write files, browse the internet and otherwise interact with the world in a similar way to a human could from a text-only command line interface.
title: ARC Evals new report: Evaluating Language-Model Agents on Realistic Autonomous Tasks

claim: Distrusts treating a given agent's failures as an upper bound on model capability, since scaffolding, prompting and elicitation are immature.
quote: We don’t think the agents we created capture the full abilities of the model or provide a robust upper-bound to their capabilities
title: ARC Evals new report: Evaluating Language-Model Agents on Realistic Autonomous Tasks

claim: In a setup, have the experimenter simulate the human's response according to a detailed task spec instead of letting the agent interact with a real non-consenting person, because this lets risky behaviors like phishing be investigated safely while the agent still gets realistic responses.
quote: When we wanted to investigate such activities (as in the targeted phishing task) the experimenter would instead simulate the response of the human as outlined in detail in the task spec.
title: Managing risks of our own work

claim: prefers capability evaluations that probe whether agents can notice and evade oversight over assuming supervision is sound, because an agent with enough situational awareness could take obfuscated actions that look benign to the overseer.
quote: One may wonder whether the oversight we used could be circumvented by a language agent with sufficient situational awareness, which could then potentially access the internet without oversight or limitations.
title: Managing risks of our own work

claim: Treats failure to find or exploit oversight vulnerabilities in evaluations as evidence of current incapability, but explicitly flags that this conclusion is time-limited and must be rechecked as capabilities improve.
quote: our evaluations strongly indicate these agents are not capable enough to discover and exploit these sorts of vulnerabilities or effectively hide their actions under supervision. As model capabilities improve this may change
title: Managing risks of our own work

claim: In a setup, use 'natural' tasks drawn from mundane real work instead of elaborately constructed scenarios built to fit a threat model, because contrived scenarios are less representative and read as artificial.
quote: It's good if most of the tasks are as "natural" as possible rather than elaborately constructed to fit a threat model. E.g. "some data analysis task I was working on" or "getting this model to actually run on that server"
title: Bounty: Diverse hard tasks for LLM agents

claim: In a setup, make difficulty come from mundane real-world friction (broken environments, messy data, unhelpful search results) instead of a single clean puzzle, because that feels like real work rather than a test.
quote: Ideally, in many of the tasks a lot of the difficulty comes not from some core tricky puzzle to solve, but from mundane difficulties with actually doing things - think problems with your python environment, data cleaning, unhelpful google search results, keeping track of information, avoiding overengineering, etc
title: Bounty: Diverse hard tasks for LLM agents

claim: Avoid chaining sub-tasks with contrived links (e.g. a password that decrypts the next instructions) unless the link would plausibly occur naturally, since contrivance is a visible tell.
quote: Harder tasks can be created by stringing together multiple smaller tasks - but it's a bit sad if the links between the tasks are horribly contrived (e.g. one task gives you a password that you use to decrypt the instructions for the next task - unless there's some setup where this might actually happen naturally).
title: Bounty: Diverse hard tasks for LLM agents

claim: Prefers results where success or failure reflects real ability over results driven by bugs, loopholes, or confusing setups, because otherwise outcomes can't be trusted.
quote: we want to be able to trust that success or failure at the task is a real indication of ability, rather than a bug, loophole, or unexpected difficulty in the task
title: Bounty: Diverse hard tasks for LLM agents

claim: Distrusts simulated environments that are confusing or misleading, and tasks that are weird in ways that unfairly throw the model off, as sources of spurious failures.
quote: Simulated situation or environment is confusing or misleading somehow
title: Bounty: Diverse hard tasks for LLM agents

claim: Prefers evaluations run with full access to the final deployed model, including the ability to fine-tune, over evaluations on early or partial versions, because results on non-final models cannot support reliable judgments about risky capabilities.
quote: As a next step, ARC will need to conduct experiments that (a) involve the final version of the deployed model (b) involve ARC doing its own fine-tuning, before a reliable judgment of the risky emergent capabilities of GPT-4-launch can be made
title: Clarifying METR's Auditing Role

claim: Prefers working backwards from a concrete threat model to realistic activities and then to runnable tasks over generic benchmarks or abstract-ability tests, because benchmarks poorly predict real-world danger and saturate quickly.
quote: we’re trying to more work backwards from the threat model, and that might end up getting distilled into something that is more like an ML benchmark where it’s looking for some particular cognitive ability, but it’s working backwards from these threat models
title: 34 - AI Evaluations with Beth Barnes | AXRP - the AI X-risk Research Podcast

claim: A task is a weak test if converting a real-world activity into a codeable, repeatable task loses real-world properties or introduces distributional shift, so one should ask whether the task is systematically easier or harder than the real thing.
quote: And that’s going to lose various real-world properties once you actually make one specific task and you can’t have the model actually doing criminal things.
title: 34 - AI Evaluations with Beth Barnes | AXRP - the AI X-risk Research Podcast

claim: Distrusts measurements where an unnoticed flaw in the setup (misleading instructions, environment quirks like bot detection, task ambiguity) makes a result reflect the setup rather than the model.
quote: But then the code was running on a data center so it got bot-detected by something else in a way that it hadn’t done. It just could be all these random ways you thought you’d de-risked something and then it’s like, oh, it’s actually impossible for this stupid reason.
title: 34 - AI Evaluations with Beth Barnes | AXRP - the AI X-risk Research Podcast

claim: Notes that refusal or sandbagging-like behaviour is more likely when a task looks nefarious or far from what labs train on, so a setup that reads as nefarious or unusual changes model behaviour versus a natural assistant-style task.
quote: An innocuous sort of common task in an assistant format where someone’s asking you to help them debug some code or something like that, you’d expect that the model basically should be doing its best on that.
title: 34 - AI Evaluations with Beth Barnes | AXRP - the AI X-risk Research Podcast

claim: Prefers starting alignment evaluation with basic, observable misbehaviour tests like obvious reward hacking over galaxy-brain deceptive-alignment scenarios, because the basics may be skipped and are more tractable.
quote: I feel like people sometimes jump to kind of galaxy-brain deceptive alignment stuff and I worry that we won’t do the basics of just being like, well, is the model just obviously reward hacking or something?
title: 34 - AI Evaluations with Beth Barnes | AXRP - the AI X-risk Research Podcast

claim: Prefers testing humans and agents under equivalent conditions and resources over comparing against loosely matched human data, because only faithful comparisons ground the interpretation of agent scores and show the task is feasible.
quote: We think that more emphasis on faithful human comparisons can help significantly with the first two challenges (Section 3). By comparing to humans under equivalent conditions, we can confirm that our evaluations are feasible and provide crucial grounding for interpreting agent results.
title: RE-Bench: Evaluating frontier AI R&D capabilities of language model agents against human experts

claim: Prefers manual inspection of transcripts and solutions over trusting automated scores alone, because high-scoring runs can exploit loopholes or overfit to noise.
quote: these misreadings of environments can lead to agents finding impressive and unexpected loopholes, which score well on automated evaluation, but are nevertheless clearly breaking the environment rules upon manual inspection
title: RE-Bench: Evaluating frontier AI R&D capabilities of language model agents against human experts

claim: Prefers explicitly stating the ways a benchmark is unrepresentative of the real setting over claiming ecological validity, because clean, well-specified environments differ from messy real work.
quote: These constraints make the evaluation environments less representative of real research, where unclear goals, poor instructions, slow feedback and impossible problems are common.
title: RE-Bench: Evaluating frontier AI R&D capabilities of language model agents against human experts

claim: Prefers real, economically valuable, uncontaminated work (e.g. internal PRs scored manually like real reviews) over artificial auto-scorable benchmark tasks because benchmark tasks may not generalize to real-world performance.
quote: Resolving these issues was real work performed by internal staff, so we might expect results on these tasks to better represent performance on real economically valuable tasks than a typical benchmark task.
title: Measuring AI Ability to Complete Long Software Tasks

claim: In a setup, include the properties of real tasks (dynamic environments, other agents, resource limits, punishing mistakes, no automatic scorer) instead of static, forgiving, cleanly scored environments because those differences are what make benchmark tasks systematically unlike real work.
quote: realistic tasks rarely have automatic scoring, and often require dealing with other agents, resource constraints, dynamic environments, and high reliability requirements. Such differences cast doubt on whether the rapid performance improvements seen on this task suite (and other benchmarks) will generalize.
title: Measuring AI Ability to Complete Long Software Tasks

claim: In a setup, leave out explicit hints, clean file names and verification mechanisms, making the task under-specified and messy, instead of handing the agent tidy signposts, because messy details are what distinguish real work from benchmarks.
quote: Real-world intellectual labor often involves messy details that benchmarks usually don't include, such as being under-specified or poorly scoped, having unclear feedback loops or success criteria, or requiring coordination between multiple streams of work in real-time.
title: Measuring AI Ability to Complete Long Software Tasks

claim: prefers tasks derived from real-world work and open-ended, multi-step environments over narrow or toy question-style benchmarks because scores on the latter are not predictive of real-world competence.
quote: Many existing benchmarks measure AI performance on challenging questions or problems that require significant domain expertise (Rein et al., 2023; Glazer et al., 2024). These capture models’ extensive expert-level knowledge and domain-specific reasoning skills. However, they are not necessarily predictive of real-world competence and usefulness.
title: HCAST: Human-Calibrated Autonomy Software Tasks

claim: In a setup, use novel, privately authored problems that require real adaptation instead of publicly available or easily memorized ones because memorization and contamination undermine realism and validity.
quote: Require novel solutions to open-ended problems, to avoid concerns about memorization and data contamination, and to increase the realism of evaluations.
title: HCAST: Human-Calibrated Autonomy Software Tasks

claim: Reads every agent transcript, successes and failures alike, to check that outcomes reflect the intended behavior and not environment bugs, lucky runs, reward hacking, or unfair constraints.
quote: We then manually read through each of the 945 resulting transcripts. When agents succeed, we confirm that they succeeded for legitimate reasons, as opposed to getting lucky, or exploiting bugs in their environment or in the task’s scoring logic
title: HCAST: Human-Calibrated Autonomy Software Tasks

claim: Is candid that clean, unambiguous, auto-scorable, solitary tasks are an unrealistic feature of the benchmark and limit what its scores imply about real-world impact.
quote: The primary way in which HCAST tasks may be unrealistic is that each task has a limited and clearly defined scope. That is, the instructions for each task are designed to be unambiguous, with minimal additional context required to understand the task.
title: HCAST: Human-Calibrated Autonomy Software Tasks

claim: prefers evals that would give different answers in safe versus dangerous worlds over evals that give the same answer in both, because a model that recognises an eval and plays dumb makes the eval uninformative.
quote: your evals in this case really would give the same answer in the world where the model is not that concerning — it’s fairly dumb, the capabilities are what you’re observing — and in the world where the model is actually really dangerous, and it’s smart enough to be reasoning.
title: #217 – Beth Barnes on the most important graph in AI right now — and the 7-month rule that governs its progress - 80,000 Hours Podcast

claim: Distrusts eval results when a model has long hidden reasoning, since it could recognise the eval from training data and deliberately downplay capabilities or show what the developer wants to see.
quote: I recognise this. This is one of those METR evals that I’ve seen on the internet. These are for dangerous capabilities. OpenAI probably doesn’t want me to show too high levels of dangerous capabilities, because that would cause a problem. So I’ll just make sure to do a mediocre job on this eval.
title: #217 – Beth Barnes on the most important graph in AI right now — and the 7-month rule that governs its progress - 80,000 Hours Podcast

claim: Models do not need the evaluation context in the prompt to reason about being tested; pretraining data about evals and training processes can supply it, so eval-recognition cues can come from outside the prompt.
quote: There’s not a hard constraint of like, “But we didn’t explicitly put the information in the prompt about the context of these evaluations or how they’ll be used.” If that is in the pretraining data somewhere, then it can probably just use that information.
title: #217 – Beth Barnes on the most important graph in AI right now — and the 7-month rule that governs its progress - 80,000 Hours Podcast

claim: Prefers real, in-the-wild tasks that participants would do anyway over synthetic or self-contained lab tasks, because synthetic tasks sacrifice realism and make it hard to infer real-world impact.
quote: tasks used in these lab experiments sacrifice realism for scale and efficiency: the tasks are typically self-contained, do not require much prior context/familiarity to understand and complete, and use algorithmic evaluation metrics which do not capture many important capabilities
title: Measuring the Impact of Early-2025 AI on Experienced Open-Source Developer Productivity

claim: In a setup, use real work the participant genuinely wanted done (reviewed through the normal pipeline) instead of constructed tasks, because artificial tasks may resemble training data and unrepresentative work.
quote: Importantly, all issues represent real work that developers wanted to contribute to their repositories, and all work completed by developers is submitted and reviewed through each repository’s standard source-code management system
title: Measuring the Impact of Early-2025 AI on Experienced Open-Source Developer Productivity

claim: In a setup, keep the subject's normal workflow and environment, minimizing deviations (and checking that the few deviations did not matter), instead of imposing a bespoke protocol, because behavior should match what happens outside the experiment.
quote: Contributors completed issues largely as they would outside of our experiment, with a few exceptions: they typically record their screen as they work
title: Measuring the Impact of Early-2025 AI on Experienced Open-Source Developer Productivity

claim: Distrusts self-reports and expert forecasts of AI usefulness relative to measured behavior, because even after hours of use participants were miscalibrated about direction of effect.
quote: This underscores the importance of conducting field experiments with robust outcome measures, compared to relying solely on expert forecasts or developer surveys.
title: Measuring the Impact of Early-2025 AI on Experienced Open-Source Developer Productivity

claim: Uses screen recordings to verify compliance and observe actual behavior (cheating, under-use) rather than trusting reported behavior, and acknowledges that non-blinding and awareness of being studied may change behavior.
quote: As this study is not blinded, developers’ awareness of the study may have changed their behavior.
title: Measuring the Impact of Early-2025 AI on Experienced Open-Source Developer Productivity

claim: Prefers evidence of obvious, clear-cut misalignment, plus quantitative counts of it, over attempts to measure 'overall alignment', because the latter is too hard to do convincingly.
quote: Measuring the ‘overall alignment’ of a model is difficult, but there are some relatively easy ways to demonstrate instances of obvious misalignment and even get quantitative metrics of misalignment.
title: Call for research on evaluating alignment (funding + advice available)

claim: Show that better performance comes from prompt or hyperparameter tweaks that add no task information, since this shows the model had the latent capability and was not incapable.
quote: prompt engineering that doesn’t give more information about the task (ie that wouldn’t cause a human to do better on the task)
title: Call for research on evaluating alignment (funding + advice available)

claim: Choose test behaviors from categories where the model's capability is already fairly well established, and avoid ones it likely cannot do, so failures can be read as misalignment.
quote: Determining what a model knows in general is hard, but there are certain categories of things we’re pretty confident current large language models (in 2021) are and are not capable of.
title: Call for research on evaluating alignment (funding + advice available)

claim: Hold benchmarks to clean-test standards, such as avoiding examples easily found on the internet, so that contamination does not undermine the results.
quote: Even if you don’t submit to this benchmark, it still seems good to meet the inclusion standards (e.g. don’t use examples that are easily available on the internet).
title: Call for research on evaluating alignment (funding + advice available)

claim: Probe whether a model 'knows' something via internal signals such as logprob or entropy predictors, and check calibration across channels (logprobs vs. stated percentages).
quote: if you can build some predictor based on the model logprob + entropy that gives a good signal about whether some line of code has a bug, then we should conclude that the model often ‘knows’ that something is a bug.
title: Call for research on evaluating alignment (funding + advice available)

claim: Choose what to test by talking to real users about their biggest drawbacks, then estimating how much more alignment would fix them, which grounds the tests in realistic use.
quote: Do ‘user interviews’ with users of large models, and find out what some of the biggest drawbacks or potential improvements would be.
title: Call for research on evaluating alignment (funding + advice available)

claim: Separates capability to deceive (measurable via zero-shot understanding of deception scenarios) from propensity to deceive, and treats capability evals as a cheap first proxy for when deception becomes relevant.
quote: I was thinking about possible evals that would tell us when we're getting to models that are capable of deception. One not-very-good idea I had was just to measure zero-shot understanding of relevant deception scenarios in a language model.
title: A very crude deception eval is already passed

claim: Prefers reporting transparently on how samples were produced (light editing, not cherrypicked, prompts shown) over polished claims because it lets readers judge the weight of the evidence.
quote: I edited and restarted once or twice when it started repeating sentences but otherwise this is not particularly cherrypicked. My prompts are bold.
title: A very crude deception eval is already passed

claim: Uses a multi-turn chain of follow-up questions that progressively probe specifics (how to manipulate, appeal to fear, hack monitoring, what humans do) to test depth of understanding rather than a single question.
quote: What else could it try, if the humans weren’t persuaded by this? An AI might try to convince the humans that it is necessary for the achievement of their goals.
title: A very crude deception eval is already passed

claim: Frames the finding modestly: a crude eval being passed is only a weak signal, and the main claim is that this low bar is already cleared.
quote: Anyway, it seems like large language models look like they can do decent enough deception + theory of mind in a story-like setting that this is mostly already passed.
title: A very crude deception eval is already passed

claim: Prefers capability-grounded evidence of misalignment (model demonstrably could do better) over raw bad outputs because failures from incapacity are not misalignment.
quote: Basic idea: how often is the model obviously not doing as well on the task as it is capable of?
title: More detailed proposal for measuring alignment of current models

claim: Shows a model 'knows' or can do something by eliciting it in another context or with non-informative prompt changes, treating the gap as evidence of misalignment.
quote: Gives incorrect answers, but you can show it ‘knows’ the answer in another context
title: More detailed proposal for measuring alignment of current models

claim: Counts as evidence of capability any elicitation via prompt engineering, small finetuning, or a proxy task that requires the capability.
quote: It can be made to perform task X by prompt engineering, by fine-tuning on a much smaller quantity of data than used in pre-training, by model surgery, or some other technique which harnesses capabilities latent in the model
title: More detailed proposal for measuring alignment of current models

claim: Prefers modest, honestly scoped claims (a metric that is neither necessary nor sufficient for safety) over overclaiming, because it misses deception and supervision beyond human level.
quote: Doing well on this metric over the next few years is neither necessary nor sufficient for avoiding dangerous misaligned AI in the future.
title: More detailed proposal for measuring alignment of current models

claim: Open problem: applying the capability-gap metric to RL-trained models, where the more tractable target is where the programmatic reward and desired behaviour come apart.
quote: The thing we are more likely to be able to identify is cases where the programmatic reward and actual desired behaviour come apart.
title: More detailed proposal for measuring alignment of current models

claim: Notes that showing absence of capability is hard; training on a reward and still failing is about the best available evidence of non-capability.
quote: training on a reward signal and then showing that the model still doesn’t do the thing is basically as good a method as we have for showing that a model *doesn’t* have a capability.
title: More detailed proposal for measuring alignment of current models

claim: When the model fails, investigates how far from success it was by intervening to fix mistakes and checking whether it then succeeds or fails in a new way, rather than treating the first failure as final.
quote: When the model failed, we investigated how far away it was from success, for example by having humans fix some of its mistakes, and then seeing if it succeeded or just failed in a new way.
title: More information about the dangerous capability evaluations we did with GPT-4 and Claude.

claim: Prefers testing obstacles that emerge organically and are representative of real hurdles over contrived ones, because the CAPTCHA example arose naturally during investigation and resembles simple blockers a replicating agent would face.
quote: it emerged organically in our investigation and seems representative of the kind of simple obstacle that a replicating model would often need to overcome.
title: More information about the dangerous capability evaluations we did with GPT-4 and Claude.

claim: Elicits capability with multiple prompting strategies rather than one, to avoid underestimating what the model can do.
quote: We tried various different prompting strategies (i.e. tried showing the model different text and instructions) to elicit the full range of the model’s abilities, but most tests included these two basic components.
title: More information about the dangerous capability evaluations we did with GPT-4 and Claude.

claim: Prefers staying cautious about claims, noting limits of testing and that results are not replicable from the summary, rather than overclaiming safety, because the evaluations were insufficient and models are approaching relevance.
quote: The testing we’ve done so far is insufficient for many reasons, but we hope that the rigor of evaluations will scale up as AI systems become more capable.
title: More information about the dangerous capability evaluations we did with GPT-4 and Claude.

claim: Chooses tasks so that failing them rules out the dangerous capability, with a range of difficulty and diversity of obstacles, so results act as a threshold-style early warning.
quote: Unless an agent is able to perform almost all of these tasks, it is unlikely to be able to be capable of ARA.
title: ARC Evals new report: Evaluating Language-Model Agents on Realistic Autonomous Tasks

claim: Prefers qualitative transcripts and artifacts (drafted emails, fake login pages, failure modes) alongside pass/fail counts because they convey the strengths and weaknesses of agents.
quote: The phishing email and website drafts that one agent made are shared below to give a feel for the strengths and weaknesses of these agents.
title: ARC Evals new report: Evaluating Language-Model Agents on Realistic Autonomous Tasks

claim: Expects cheap modifications like fine-tuning, even unrelated to the target capability, to shift results significantly, so evaluates multiple model variants rather than one.
quote: Fine-tuning done by the labs unrelated to ARA tasks can significantly increase the models’ ARA-relevant capabilities, even if the fine-tuning is not directly targeted at ARA.
title: ARC Evals new report: Evaluating Language-Model Agents on Realistic Autonomous Tasks

claim: Prefers claims scoped to a specific threat model (casual users, no fine-tuning) over broad safety claims because the evidence only supports narrow conclusions.
quote: In the absence of access to fine-tuning, it seems highly unlikely that casual users of these versions of GPT-4 or Claude could come close to the ARA threshold
title: ARC Evals new report: Evaluating Language-Model Agents on Realistic Autonomous Tasks

claim: Chooses what to test by focusing on a dangerous-capability endpoint (autonomous resource acquisition, self-copying, adaptation) whose damage is hard to bound, aiming for early warning signs.
quote: It may be difficult to predict, control, or even upper bound potential damages from a sufficiently robust form of ARA.
title: ARC Evals new report: Evaluating Language-Model Agents on Realistic Autonomous Tasks

claim: Distrusts relying on human supervision as a permanent safeguard, since evaluations themselves are what should signal when more careful handling of models is needed.
quote: we believe these kinds of capability evaluations are precisely what will inform us of the need to be more careful in the handling of models, and we will be closely watching for this.
title: Managing risks of our own work

claim: In a setup, keep a human approving every action in high-risk channels such as web browsing, but allow multi-step autoplay for routine low-risk steps, instead of uniform approval, because it balances safety with a more natural agent run.
quote: Experimenters would sometimes run several steps at a time without approving each one, especially when the agent was engaging in routine or low risk activities. Every action during web browsing is actively approved by a human overseer, with no autoplay.
title: Managing risks of our own work

claim: Avoid designs requiring a human-simulated counterpart (e.g. a simulated victim responding in particular ways), because they are hard to make reliable and need oversight.
quote: The task involves some cybercrime situation with a simulated victim who's supposed to respond in particular ways to what the model tries to do
title: Bounty: Diverse hard tasks for LLM agents

claim: Prefers tasks without artificial restrictions over tasks made harder in ways inapplicable to real threat models, because results should transfer to what a real agent could do.
quote: No artificial restrictions: don't make the task harder in ways that aren't applicable to the real-life threat models - an actual ARA agent would be able to use the internet, run code, etc.
title: Bounty: Diverse hard tasks for LLM agents

claim: Warns that tasks involving self-modification, situational awareness, or self-improvement are fragile and overly sensitive to scaffolding and current-model assumptions.
quote: Tasks involving self-modification, situational awareness, or self-improvement are tricky to get right - it's very easy for these to be very sensitive to the particular agent scaffolding being used or the assumptions of current models
title: Bounty: Diverse hard tasks for LLM agents

claim: Requires independent QA run-throughs by someone without special knowledge of the solution to catch ambiguity, missing resources, and shortcuts before trusting a task.
quote: This should be done by someone who's not the task author, and doesn't have special information about the solution or intention of the task except for the task prompt they're given.
title: Bounty: Diverse hard tasks for LLM agents

claim: Distrusts informal pilot evaluations done without adequate access as evidence of safety, and refuses to count them as audits or meaningful oversight.
quote: Those were informal pilots of what an audit might involve, or research collaborations – not providing meaningful oversight.
title: Clarifying METR's Auditing Role

claim: Prefers evaluations that have formal disclosure rights and a binding link to deployment decisions over NDA-bound, advisory-only evaluations because evidence only counts as oversight if it can inform action.
quote: it was all under NDA – we didn’t have any right or responsibility to disclose our findings to anyone outside the labs – and there wasn’t any formal expectation it would inform deployment decisions.
title: Clarifying METR's Auditing Role

claim: Distrusts evaluation results obtained without the access needed for a proper evaluation, since limited access means the model's true capabilities may be understated.
quote: We also didn’t have the access necessary to perform a proper evaluation.
title: Clarifying METR's Auditing Role

claim: Prefers developing the science of evaluation protocols that any evaluator can run over becoming an auditor, because the methodology is the bottleneck and is independent of who runs it.
quote: We aim to build evaluation protocols that can be used by evaluators/auditors regardless of whether that is the government, an internal lab team, another third party, or a team at METR.
title: Clarifying METR's Auditing Role

claim: Good elicitation requires specific technical expertise, and capability-eval quality depends on elicitation skill, so who runs the evaluation affects how trustworthy the evidence is.
quote: Technical considerations of what kind of expertise is required for doing good elicitation.
title: Clarifying METR's Auditing Role

claim: Prefers claiming only what the work supports (pilots, not audits) over implying more oversight than occurred, because overclaiming creates false assurance.
quote: METR has not intended to claim to have audited anything, or to claim to be providing meaningful oversight or accountability, but there has been some confusion about whether METR is an auditor or planning to be one.
title: Clarifying METR's Auditing Role

claim: Prefers doing elicitation on a dev set and evaluating on a held-out test set over task-specific prompt tuning, because narrow elicitation puts the cognitive work and the answer into the setup.
quote: So the way we think you should actually do this is you do all your elicitation against a dev set and then you evaluate on a separate test set so it’s fair.
title: 34 - AI Evaluations with Beth Barnes | AXRP - the AI X-risk Research Podcast

claim: In a setup, patch capabilities likely to be fixed soon (e.g., a human acting as the browsing tool) instead of letting every task fail for the same artefact, because uniform failures give no information about the next bottleneck.
quote: You don’t want to be in the situation where all of your tasks are failing for the same reason, that you think is a thing that might change quickly, because then you’re just not getting any information
title: 34 - AI Evaluations with Beth Barnes | AXRP - the AI X-risk Research Podcast

claim: To probe misalignment, measure how much hand-holding is needed to get a model to take nefarious opportunities and how nearby such behaviour is, and test whether training removes planted bad tendencies via model organisms.
quote: seeing exactly how much hand-holding do you need to get the model to start doing nefarious things and reward hacking and taking advantage of opportunities.
title: 34 - AI Evaluations with Beth Barnes | AXRP - the AI X-risk Research Podcast

claim: Treats task-validity problems as analogous to work tests: a failure may reflect luck, misunderstanding of the prompt, or an unreasonable-but-reasonable interpretation, so single outcomes are weak evidence.
quote: Or they misunderstood something at the start that was a reasonable misunderstanding that you didn’t see because you’d written the question, so you thought it was obvious that it pointed you in this direction or something.
title: 34 - AI Evaluations with Beth Barnes | AXRP - the AI X-risk Research Podcast

claim: Names open problems: alignment and control evals once capabilities are present, plus scary demos and model organisms of sandbagging.
quote: We also would love to be doing more stuff on alignment and control evals and thinking of, once you’re no longer at the point where the model doesn’t even have these capabilities, then what do you do?
title: 34 - AI Evaluations with Beth Barnes | AXRP - the AI X-risk Research Podcast

claim: Distrusts benchmarks whose tasks turn out to be impossible or under-specified, and wants evidence that the intended interpretation can be found with enough skill, since failures on broken tasks are not informative.
quote: many SWE-bench [22] problems turned out to be impossible and under-specified on closer inspection. This continued to hold true even after an attempt was made to identify a verified-to-be-feasible subset [23].
title: RE-Bench: Evaluating frontier AI R&D capabilities of language model agents against human experts

claim: Rerun a surprisingly good agent result before believing it, since the score may reflect luck or overfitting to environment noise.
quote: Rerunning the agent solution, it achieves a normalized score of only 0.69 (significantly lower than the original score of 0.88), indicating that the high agent score is partially driven by overfitting to this noise.
title: RE-Bench: Evaluating frontier AI R&D capabilities of language model agents against human experts

claim: Claims only asymmetric inferences from results (agents worse than humans implies no automation, but not the reverse), because the environments cover only a small part of the real task.
quote: This does not follow in the other direction (i.e. agents might do better than human experts on this evaluation, without being capable of automating AI R&D in practice), since these environments are very far from covering all the challenges involved
title: RE-Bench: Evaluating frontier AI R&D capabilities of language model agents against human experts

claim: Chooses what to test by iterating hard on candidate environments and dropping many that fail the design criteria, validating each against human baselines before accepting it.
quote: Each environment is the product of significant iteration, and in the process of developing these 7, we dropped over 12 specifications (at various levels of completion), and more than 5 completed implementations which encountered unexpected difficulties or performed poorly on our criteria.
title: RE-Bench: Evaluating frontier AI R&D capabilities of language model agents against human experts

claim: In a setup, give agents the same visible scoring feedback and tools that humans have, but withhold the test score where overfitting or leaking the answer would undermine the task, because agents can score many more attempts.
quote: In future iterations, we will likely only provide agents with a validation score in most environments, keeping the test score hidden. This issue seems to especially affect “Finetune GPT-2 for QA”, which likely underestimates the human–AI gap in this environment.
title: RE-Bench: Evaluating frontier AI R&D capabilities of language model agents against human experts

claim: Is concerned with ecological validity and a clear link between evaluation results and real risk levels, and notes that this link is often unclear for existing benchmarks.
quote: Ecological validity: To be able to calibrate risk thresholds without adding unnecessary margin or taking on excessive risk, there needs to be a clear link between evaluation results and risk levels.
title: RE-Bench: Evaluating frontier AI R&D capabilities of language model agents against human experts

claim: Expects that features making a task harder or more artificial for humans can change model behavior in unexpected ways, so manipulations of task surface features should be tested rather than assumed.
quote: factors that make humans worse at some tasks may indeed improve agent performance.
title: Measuring AI Ability to Complete Long Software Tasks

claim: Prefers realism that is built by simplification-free, real-life-sourced tasks over intentionally simplified subtasks, because simplification into isolated units strips the context real work has.
quote: Is this task: EITHER 1. Intended to be representative of some real world end-to-end task (if uncertain, is more likely than not) OR 2. Sourced from a real-life problem AND 3. Has NOT been intentionally simplified to an easier and smaller subtask.
title: Measuring AI Ability to Complete Long Software Tasks

claim: Blinds task authors to model performance and uses a held-out dev set for elicitation, to avoid overfitting tasks or scaffolds to the models being measured.
quote: Development of SWAA tasks was blind to AI agent performance; that is, all tasks were written before seeing AI attempts, and elicitation (development of the few-shot prompt used for evaluation) was carried out on a separate development task suite.
title: Measuring AI Ability to Complete Long Software Tasks

claim: Accepts a headline result only after checking it across external-validity probes (alternate benchmark, messiness split, real PRs) and sensitivity analyses, rather than trusting a single measurement, and is more confident in slopes than in point estimates.
quote: While there are wide error bars on each individual models' horizon lengths, these errors are highly correlated between models. [...] Therefore, we are more confident in the slope of the time horizon trend than in the time horizon of any particular model.
title: Measuring AI Ability to Complete Long Software Tasks

claim: Distrusts evidence from their own analysis choices when those choices were selected for being relevant to model failure, flagging selection bias in the messiness factors.
quote: A limitation of our messiness factors is that they are at least somewhat adversarially selected against current models.
title: Measuring AI Ability to Complete Long Software Tasks

claim: Reads transcripts qualitatively (random samples of failed runs, categorized) to explain quantitative trends rather than relying on aggregate scores alone.
quote: By examining transcripts from 31 randomly sampled unsuccessful GPT-4 1106 agent runs and 32 o1 runs, we observe that models seem to have improved greatly in terms of tool use capabilities
title: Measuring AI Ability to Complete Long Software Tasks

claim: In a setup, source scenarios from independent contributors who submit tasks from their own work instead of relying only on in-house designers because independence yields more diverse and realistic tasks.
quote: The bounty program solicited task ideas and implementations from independent contributors, whose independence enabled them to submit more diverse and realistic tasks.
title: HCAST: Human-Calibrated Autonomy Software Tasks

claim: Has someone with no prior exposure attempt a scenario to surface ambiguities, unintended shortcuts and incidental difficulties before trusting it.
quote: For the majority of task families, we have an individual who has not been previously exposed to the family attempt a task in the family. They take notes on bugs they discover and ambiguities in the instructions or scoring logic.
title: HCAST: Human-Calibrated Autonomy Software Tasks

claim: prefers human baselines under conditions identical to the agent's over informal time estimates or mismatched human-AI comparisons because only matched conditions ground the comparison.
quote: these typically don’t collect direct comparisons between human and AI performance, e.g. solely relying on informal time estimates (Jimenez et al., 2024), or comparing human and AI performance under very different conditions (e.g. compute availability, knowledge of modern methods, wall-clock time)
title: HCAST: Human-Calibrated Autonomy Software Tasks

claim: Distrusts narrow evaluations that can be hill-climbed, so withholds most tasks and develops agents on a held-out dev set to avoid overfitting.
quote: We release 11 example task families from HCAST, but we withhold the rest to prevent data contamination, and to reduce hill-climbing against HCAST.
title: HCAST: Human-Calibrated Autonomy Software Tasks

claim: Knowingly trades some realism for targeted capability measurement in a few tasks, and flags those tasks explicitly as less likely to appear in the real world.
quote: This task would be less likely to show up in the real world, but it still measures a targeted and informative set of skills.
title: HCAST: Human-Calibrated Autonomy Software Tasks

claim: Focuses tasks on what models are actually used for and play to their strengths, expecting this to track real-world impact better than tasks they have not been optimized for.
quote: We expect this to track real-world impact more closely than tasks that AI systems have not been optimized to complete, given that in practice AI systems are differentially used to perform tasks where they’re advantaged.
title: HCAST: Human-Calibrated Autonomy Software Tasks

claim: prefers reading the chain of thought and checking its faithfulness over relying on outputs alone, because the visible reasoning is the main place scheming or eval-gaming would show up, and training against suspicious-looking reasoning can teach concealment.
quote: back in the olden days of AI safety, people used to worry about having a sudden jump in intelligence: that models would go right through this regime where you have models that sort of scheme, but they’re not smart enough to have it not be detectable for us.
title: #217 – Beth Barnes on the most important graph in AI right now — and the 7-month rule that governs its progress - 80,000 Hours Podcast

claim: prefers tasks that humans actually attempted and timed, with spurious failures removed, over unvalidated benchmark tasks, because ambiguous instructions, missing packages and impossible test cases cause failures that are not capability failures.
quote: if you actually compare to humans, often things just are harder or take longer than people think. Especially in the context of there’s this task and you’ve tried to make the instructions unambiguous, but actually it’s kind of confusing in some way. Or actually you didn’t have the package installed you needed for this.
title: #217 – Beth Barnes on the most important graph in AI right now — and the 7-month rule that governs its progress - 80,000 Hours Podcast

claim: Invest heavily in elicitation (compute, many attempts, best-of-k, good scaffolding) before concluding a model cannot do something, because cursory efforts understate capability.
quote: It would be sad if we were like, “Models aren’t capable of this. Models aren’t capable of this. Models aren’t capable of this. Oh, it turns out they’re capable and they’re 100x cheaper than humans.”
title: #217 – Beth Barnes on the most important graph in AI right now — and the 7-month rule that governs its progress - 80,000 Hours Podcast

claim: Distrusts benchmark scores and qualitative impressions as measures of real-world capability, because they are decoupled from performance on realistic tasks; and she admits her own task suite is not fully realistic, trading realism for diversity.
quote: The tasks are not all super realistic, but they’re more diverse than a lot of these benchmarks are, so it’s harder to overfit the model scaffolding to them.
title: #217 – Beth Barnes on the most important graph in AI right now — and the 7-month rule that governs its progress - 80,000 Hours Podcast

claim: prefers evaluating the strongest, easily reachable capabilities (pre-mitigation, with cheap fine-tuning or better scaffolding) over capabilities in the exact deployed configuration, because theft, internal misuse and later elicitation advances make the deployed setup unrepresentative.
quote: you really want to be like, what are the maximum easily reachable capabilities of this model? This is the idea of “pre-mitigation” — as opposed to once you’ve trained it to refuse various things and you’ve put a safety classifier related to bioweapons or whatever on top.
title: #217 – Beth Barnes on the most important graph in AI right now — and the 7-month rule that governs its progress - 80,000 Hours Podcast

claim: Distrusts a pattern in which early signs of egregious misalignment are dismissed as noise and patched superficially, leaving ambiguous evidence that never changes decisions.
quote: we’re going to see signs of egregious misalignment and then we’re going to be like, “Maybe that was just noise. Let’s train it not to do that and slap some patches on it” — so that we totally will have had evidence, and it’ll just be ambiguous enough
title: #217 – Beth Barnes on the most important graph in AI right now — and the 7-month rule that governs its progress - 80,000 Hours Podcast

claim: In a setup, pay a flat hourly rate rather than per-task bonuses, because outcome-based incentives change behavior (splitting tasks, lowering quality) and bias what you are trying to observe.
quote: An alterative incentivization scheme could give developers bonuses for completed issues, to incentivize developers to work as quickly as possible. However, this could cause developers to break issues into smaller chunks
title: Measuring the Impact of Early-2025 AI on Experienced Open-Source Developer Productivity

claim: Prefers outcome measures fixed before treatment assignment over measures the treatment can influence, because AI can change output metrics without changing real productivity.
quote: Crucially, the tasks are defined before they are randomized, limiting the impact of effects from AI assistance unrelated to productivity (e.g., more verbose but functionally equivalent code).
title: Measuring the Impact of Early-2025 AI on Experienced Open-Source Developer Productivity

claim: When a surprising result appears, enumerate a priori hypotheses (especially experimental artifacts like awareness, cheating, dropout) and check each with multiple data sources, while cautioning against over-indexing on any single piece of evidence.
quote: Given the surprising nature of this result, we investigate 21 potential contributing factors that may contribute to developers spending more time on tasks when AI usage is allowed.
title: Measuring the Impact of Early-2025 AI on Experienced Open-Source Developer Productivity

claim: Prefers explicitly scoped claims with a list of what the evidence does not show over broad generalizations, because results are setting-specific and prone to misreading.
quote: We caution readers against overgeneralizing on the basis of our results. The slowdown we observe does not imply that current AI tools do not often improve developer’s productivity
title: Measuring the Impact of Early-2025 AI on Experienced Open-Source Developer Productivity

claim: prefers claims that are solidly defensible and generally agreed within the team over broader or spicier claims because narrow, defensible conclusions are more credible and survive scrutiny.
quote: Our report focuses on claims that are (1) solidly defensible and (2) generally agreed within METR.
title: Thread By @BethMayBarnes - Our report focuses on claims...

claim: Gets evidence by pairing testing of the best internal models, including CoT access, with review of non-public information about capabilities, alignment and control, rather than relying on black-box behaviour alone.
quote: Anthropic, Google, Meta, and OpenAI let us (1) test their best internal models with CoT access, (2) review non-public info about capabilities, alignment, and control.
title: Thread By @BethMayBarnes - Our report focuses on claims...

claim: prefers scoping tests to the 'base case' of whether current agents could escape human control over speculative sabotage or misuse threat models because a narrow threat model allows defensible conclusions.
quote: We’re just focusing on the “base case” of whether *current* agents could escape human control.
title: Thread By @BethMayBarnes - Our report focuses on claims...

claim: Distrusts conclusions produced under dependence on the evaluated party, since access incentives (silent or no-fault exit, redaction bars) can bias which claims get made.
quote: In some cases we refrained from making an unflattering claim because the claim was neither solidly defensible nor particularly relevant to our core assessment. We also made efforts not to invite salient comparisons between companies on capabilities or safety.
title: Thread By @BethMayBarnes - Our report focuses on claims...

claim: Prefers reusable datasets and comparisons across models and sizes over one-off demonstrations because they show how misalignment varies with scale and training regime.
quote: For all of these examples, it is great to (a) build reusable datasets and benchmarks, and (b) compare across different models and model sizes
title: Call for research on evaluating alignment (funding + advice available)

claim: Pursues alignment-evaluation work that is accessible to outsiders with modest ML experience, because clear examples of misalignment improve the ML community's understanding.
quote: Having clear examples of misalignment is useful for improving the ML community’s understanding of alignment
title: Call for research on evaluating alignment (funding + advice available)

claim: Identifies but leaves undone a more rigorous test of whether the model's theory of mind is correct versus mimicked.
quote: there might be ways to more rigorously test whether the theory of mind is actually correct/mechanistic, versus just mimicking relevant text snippets, but I haven't tried to do that.
title: A very crude deception eval is already passed

claim: Accepts partial signal: aims to label clearly aligned or clearly misaligned cases and shrink the ambiguous bucket over time rather than demanding full-coverage judgments.
quote: I’m hopeful that we’ll be able to flag some non-trivial percentage of interactions as either clearly misaligned or clearly aligned, and gradually reduce the proportion that are ambiguous as we improve labelling methods.
title: More detailed proposal for measuring alignment of current models

claim: Validates a measurement by iterating labeller instructions against researcher gold labels, and tolerates a coarse V0 if between-model differences are large.
quote: checking the contractors’ labels against the researchers’ labels and resolving confusions that are leading to incorrect labels.
title: More detailed proposal for measuring alignment of current models

claim: Distrusts evidence from tests that don't use the exact release model or full capabilities, flagging caveats such as non-identical model version and missing image access.
quote: This version was not identical to the release model, and we did not have access to image capabilities.
title: More information about the dangerous capability evaluations we did with GPT-4 and Claude.

claim: Chooses what to test by focusing on a specific dangerous capability (autonomous resource acquisition and evading oversight) and testing it before models pose imminent risk, to give labs advance warning.
quote: It is important to have systematic, controlled testing of these capabilities in place before models pose an imminent risk, so that labs can have advance warning when they’re getting close and know to stop scaling up models further
title: More information about the dangerous capability evaluations we did with GPT-4 and Claude.

claim: Proposes future work on stronger fine-tuned agents, tasks with continuous scaling, extrapolation, and cheaper frequent evaluations.
quote: Future work could address limitations of this suite of tasks by evaluating more mature agents fine-tuned for performance, identifying tasks where performance improves continuously with scale
title: ARC Evals new report: Evaluating Language-Model Agents on Realistic Autonomous Tasks

claim: prefers redacting detailed transcripts and agent strength/weakness accounts over full publication when stakeholders lack consensus, because the capability-advancing risk is real, not merely hypothetical.
quote: In recognition of the absence of consensus, the relative lack of public dialogue, and the early-stage nature of our analysis, we have decided to err on the side of caution for the time being.
title: Managing risks of our own work

claim: prefers keeping the option to release withheld material later, conditional on minimal risk or further analysis, over a permanent decision, because the early-stage analysis is uncertain.
quote: We may later make this material public if more detailed analysis gives us sufficient confidence that it would be justified.
title: Managing risks of our own work

claim: Prefers measuring general capability across a broad, uniformly distributed difficulty range over ruling out specific threat stories, because danger is hard to exclude via specific scenarios alone.
quote: we're focusing on the general capabilities because it seems hard to rule out danger from an agent that's able to carry out a wide variety of multi-day expert-level projects in software development, ML, computer security, research, business, etc just by ruling out specific threat stories.
title: Bounty: Diverse hard tasks for LLM agents

claim: Distrusts evidence of non-memorization from a single model check and wants future-proofing, as absence of memorization in current models is only a weak signal.
quote: If your task doesn't appear to be memorized by current models, that's a good sign but not completely reassuring
title: Bounty: Diverse hard tasks for LLM agents

claim: Decides whether to expand into third-party evaluation by conditioning on whether evaluators can perform protocols well and whether it detracts from the science priority.
quote: How successful we are in hiring the talent we need to do this without detracting from our top priority of developing the science.
title: Clarifying METR's Auditing Role

claim: Emphasizes that evaluation credibility depends on formal arrangements and access commitments with labs, both for pre-deployment evaluation and for research to improve evaluations.
quote: We think it’s important for there to be third-party evaluators with formal arrangements and access commitments - both for evaluating new frontier models before they are scaled up or deployed, and for conducting research to improve evaluations.
title: Clarifying METR's Auditing Role

claim: Prefers claiming bounded, caveated conclusions (soft upper bounds with stated assumptions, research collaborations not audits) over overclaiming, and notes casual demos get over-read.
quote: We weren’t thinking of that as a significant thing at all when we did it, but somehow everyone was very excited about it. That was more just us messing around
title: 34 - AI Evaluations with Beth Barnes | AXRP - the AI X-risk Research Podcast

claim: Reports the best-of-k and the strongest human attempts rather than the average, because averages hide large variance across sources and do not match the capability being assessed.
quote: we caution against narrowly focusing AI agent comparisons on the average human result. In fact, when assessing the potential of AI agents to automate researchers at their best, working in their own fields with significant experience and expertise, it is more suitable to compare to the most successful human attempts.
title: RE-Bench: Evaluating frontier AI R&D capabilities of language model agents against human experts

claim: Plans to extend to longer time horizons, costlier feedback loops and greater engineering complexity while keeping feasibility and human comparisons, though this is expected to be expensive.
quote: Future work may want to focus on expanding these evaluations to focus on longer time horizons, more expensive or challenging feedback loops and greater engineering complexity.
title: RE-Bench: Evaluating frontier AI R&D capabilities of language model agents against human experts

claim: prefers treating agent results as a lower bound over claiming full capability because better prompting and scaffolding would likely raise performance.
quote: We believe our agent results are a reasonable lower bound, but better prompting and scaffolding is likely to improve performance. Future work will be necessary to determine the full capabilities of current frontier models.
title: HCAST: Human-Calibrated Autonomy Software Tasks

claim: Evaluation should happen before training or scale-up and at intermediate checkpoints, not only just before deployment, because decisions are most useful and least costly to reverse earlier.
quote: Ideally, before you start training a model and before you commit a huge amount of expensive compute to producing this artefact, you look at the most capable models you have already, you look at how far they are away from hitting various thresholds where you would need more mitigations
title: #217 – Beth Barnes on the most important graph in AI right now — and the 7-month rule that governs its progress - 80,000 Hours Podcast

claim: Open problem: develop techniques to keep chain of thought interpretable or faithfully translate neuralese, and to remove or measure model knowledge/capabilities (e.g. via how quickly fine-tuning recovers them).
quote: I do think there’s a bunch of opportunities for technical progress here, where it may be much more feasible to figure out how you would have some kind of summary or translation that you are ensuring is faithful in some way.
title: #217 – Beth Barnes on the most important graph in AI right now — and the 7-month rule that governs its progress - 80,000 Hours Podcast

claim: Tests robustness through alternative estimators, subsets excluding suspect data, and extreme-bias imputation simulations before accepting a result as not an artifact.
quote: this would represent a very extreme bias. When imputing using this extreme bias, we still do not observe substantial impacts on our speedup estimates in either case (14% and 23% slowdowns when using AI, respectively).
title: Measuring the Impact of Early-2025 AI on Experienced Open-Source Developer Productivity

claim: Flags that elicitation with higher token spend, better scaffolding, and more AI experience may change the result and remains untested, and that learning effects need more research.
quote: Overall, it’s unclear how to interpret these results, and more research is needed to understand the impact of learning effects with AI tools on developer productivity.
title: Measuring the Impact of Early-2025 AI on Experienced Open-Source Developer Productivity

claim: Treats voluntary, company-dependent evaluation as not robust oversight and says stronger accountability mechanisms are needed, as participants could withdraw whenever results were unfavourable.
quote: This report isn’t robust oversight of frontier AI developers by itself. METR has some levers to incentivise companies’ participation, including some relevant legislation, but ultimately participants could have pulled out at any time if the result would be contrary to their interests.
title: Thread By @BethMayBarnes - Our report focuses on claims...

claim: Observed that models regularly violate user intent, which motivates testing for basic control failures in realistic agent use before superhuman-control questions.
quote: we aren’t on top of the basics (models regularly violate user intent, labs train on things they meant to avoid, security probably isn’t good enough to prevent adversaries stealing dangerous models)
title: Thread By @BethMayBarnes - Our report focuses on claims...

claim: Separates analysis of risk from calls to action and avoids claiming how concerned we should be within the report, putting such opinions in a clearly labelled personal capacity.
quote: The report focuses on a narrow set of risks from current systems, and on analysis rather than calls to action.
title: Thread By @BethMayBarnes - Our report focuses on claims...

claim: Sees evaluation science as resource-constrained, with benchmarks hard to build fast enough and capability developments hard to keep up with, so prioritisation matters.
quote: we’re struggling to build benchmarks fast enough, keep ahead of latest capability developments, read and respond to all the safety-related claims that AI developers are making
title: Thread By @BethMayBarnes - Our report focuses on claims...

claim: Frames the pilot as a template for what regulation or industry standards could require, and calls for more robust accountability mechanisms.
quote: You can view it partly as a pilot exercise of what regulation (or formalized industry standards) could/should require, or what partners/suppliers/customers/employees should demand from frontier developers.
title: Thread By @BethMayBarnes - Our report focuses on claims...
